CUSTOMER LISTS AS TRADE SECRETS UNDER CUTSA — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Bayline Roofing Services, Inc.

PURPOSE OF THIS CUSTOMER LISTS AS TRADE SECRETS INFORMATION SHEET
This Information Sheet describes how California law treats a business's customer list -- the names, contact information, and related data about the customers it has developed -- as a potential trade secret under the California Uniform Trade Secrets Act (Civ. Code, § 3426 et seq.). It sets out the statutory definition of a trade secret in Civil Code section 3426.1, subdivision (d), and the definition of misappropriation in subdivision (b); the California Court of Appeal's explanations of when a customer list derives independent economic value from not being generally known (ABBA Rubber Co. v. Seaquist; Morlife, Inc. v. Perry); the rule that ease of ascertainability is not part of California's statutory definition but remains available as a defense (ABBA Rubber); the kinds of evidence courts have treated as reasonable efforts to maintain secrecy (Morlife); the distinction between soliciting a former employer's customers and merely announcing a new affiliation; and the boundary between trade secret protection and the general rule against contractual restraints on competition in Business and Professions Code section 16600. It is prepared by Jordan T. Reyes concerning the customer information of Bayline Roofing Services, Inc., described as follows: A database of approximately 400 commercial property managers who have purchased roof maintenance services since 2019, including contact persons, pricing history, and service notes. This Information Sheet describes what the statutes and cited decisions say; it does not itself determine whether the customer information described above is a trade secret, whether any person has misappropriated it, or what remedies would be available in any specific dispute, and it is not a substitute for that case-specific legal determination.

THE BASELINE RULE: A FORMER EMPLOYEE MAY COMPETE FOR FORMER CUSTOMERS, BUT MAY NOT USE TRADE SECRETS TO DO SO
California law starts from the premise that a former employee may go into business in competition with a former employer and may compete for the business of that employer's customers. In Morlife, Inc. v. Perry, the Court of Appeal quoted the California Supreme Court's statement in Continental Car-Na-Var Corp. v. Moseley that a former employee has the right to engage in a competitive business and to compete with the former employer even for the business of its former customers, provided the competition is fairly and legally conducted. The same court framed the limit on that freedom in a single sentence: a former employee may use the general knowledge, skill, and experience acquired in the former employment, but may not use confidential information or trade secrets in doing so. The customer-list cases described in this Information Sheet are about where that line falls.

THE STATUTORY DEFINITION OF A TRADE SECRET (CIVIL CODE § 3426.1(D))
The California Uniform Trade Secrets Act defines a trade secret as information -- the statute lists a formula, pattern, compilation, program, device, method, technique, or process as examples -- that satisfies two requirements: it derives independent economic value, actual or potential, from not being generally known to the public or to other persons who can obtain economic value from its disclosure or use, and it is the subject of efforts that are reasonable under the circumstances to maintain its secrecy. A customer list is not named in the statute's list of examples, but the list is introduced by the word "including" and the courts have treated a compilation of customer information as a kind of information that can meet the definition, as described in the clauses that follow. The definition also uses the phrase "generally known," and does not use the phrase "readily ascertainable"; the significance of that omission is addressed in a separate clause.

A CUSTOMER LIST CAN QUALIFY AS A TRADE SECRET; THE THREE ELEMENTS
In ABBA Rubber Co. v. Seaquist, the Court of Appeal read the statutory definition as consisting of three elements: information, which is valuable because it is unknown to others, and which the owner has attempted to keep secret. The court stated that a customer list is one of the types of information which can qualify as a trade secret, and noted that the defendants in that case did not claim otherwise. In the case before it -- a preliminary injunction obtained by a manufacturer of rubber rollers against a former manager who had gone to work for a competitor -- the defendants conceded that substantial evidence supported the finding that the plaintiff took reasonable steps to keep its customer information secret, so the dispute centered on the second element: whether the list's value derived from the fact that it was not generally known to competitors.

ECONOMIC VALUE MUST COME FROM SECRECY: VALUE TO THE OWNER ALONE IS NOT ENOUGH
The ABBA Rubber court explained that showing a customer list is valuable to the business that owns it does not by itself satisfy the statute, because a list of the persons who have paid for a business's goods or services will always have value to that business. The statute instead requires that the information have value to competitors who do not know it and could put it to use. The court illustrated the point with a hypothetical widget market: a seller's list of 500 businesses that have bought widgets is a protectable trade secret if competitors do not know which of the 100,000 businesses in widget-using industries actually buy widgets, because the list tells competitors where to target their sales efforts; but if competitors already know that those 500 businesses are widget consumers (even without knowing that they buy from that particular seller), the list has no independent economic value. As the court put it, in both situations the identities of the seller's own customers are unknown, and the distinguishing factor is whether it is also unknown that those businesses buy the product at all. Morlife, Inc. v. Perry made the same point in different words: a customer list can be found to have economic value because its disclosure would let a competitor direct its sales efforts to customers who have already shown a willingness to use a particular type of service or product, rather than to people who only might be interested.

LISTS BUILT THROUGH TIME AND EFFORT VERSUS LISTS ANYONE COULD ASSEMBLE
The Morlife court described a general pattern in the California decisions: courts are reluctant to protect customer lists to the extent they embody information that is readily ascertainable through public sources such as business directories, but where the employer has expended time and effort identifying customers with particular needs or characteristics, courts will prohibit former employees from using that information to capture a share of the market. In the case before it, the court relied on testimony that the roofing company's customers were discoverable only with great effort, that it built its customer base through telemarketing, sales visits, mailings, advertising, trade-association membership, referrals, and research, and that only about 10 of every 100 telemarketing contacts produced a lead. The court also noted, in a footnote, that the customer information at issue was not a physical list but a compilation of names, addresses, and data derived from business cards removed from the employer's premises and from the former employee's memory.

"READILY ASCERTAINABLE" IS NOT PART OF CALIFORNIA'S DEFINITION, BUT REMAINS A DEFENSE
In ABBA Rubber Co. v. Seaquist, the defendants argued that the identities of the plaintiff's customers could not be a trade secret because they were readily ascertainable from trade directories, telephone books, and similar sources. The Court of Appeal rejected the argument as a matter of statutory text. The Uniform Trade Secrets Act as proposed by the National Conference of Commissioners on Uniform State Laws defines a trade secret as information deriving value from not being generally known to, "and not being readily ascertainable by proper means by," others; when the California Legislature enacted the definition as Civil Code section 3426.1, subdivision (d)(1), it deleted that phrase. The court read the deletion to mean that the Legislature chose to exclude from the definition only information the industry already knows, as opposed to information the industry could easily discover, so that under California law information can be a trade secret even though it is readily ascertainable, so long as it has not yet been ascertained by others in the industry. The court declined to follow an earlier decision (American Paper & Packaging Products, Inc. v. Kirgan) to the extent it suggested otherwise. In a footnote, however, the court explained -- citing the Legislature's committee comment -- that the assertion that a matter is readily ascertainable by proper means remains available as a defense to a claim of misappropriation: if the defendants could show that the customers were easily identifiable and that their knowledge of the plaintiff's customers came from that identification process rather than from the plaintiff's records, the defense would rest on the absence of misappropriation rather than the absence of a trade secret.

EVIDENCE OF REASONABLE EFFORTS TO MAINTAIN SECRECY
The second statutory requirement is that the information be the subject of efforts that are reasonable under the circumstances to maintain its secrecy. In Morlife, Inc. v. The court cautioned that labeling information a trade secret or confidential does not conclusively establish that it is one, but treated such labeling as an important factor in showing the value the employer placed on the information and that it could not be readily derived from public sources. The court also repeated an earlier holding that, to afford protection to the employer, the information need not be in writing but may be in the employee's memory.

MISAPPROPRIATION: DISCLOSURE OR USE, AND WHAT COUNTS AS IMPROPER MEANS (CIVIL CODE § 3426.1(A)-(B))
Proving that a customer list is a trade secret is only the first step; the owner must also prove misappropriation. The statute defines misappropriation to include acquisition of a trade secret by a person who knows or has reason to know it was acquired by improper means, and disclosure or use of a trade secret without express or implied consent by a person who, among other alternatives, used improper means to acquire it, or who at the time of disclosure or use knew or had reason to know that his or her knowledge of it was acquired under circumstances giving rise to a duty to maintain its secrecy or limit its use. "Improper means" is defined to include theft, bribery, misrepresentation, breach or inducement of a breach of a duty to maintain secrecy, or espionage through electronic or other means -- but the statute expressly provides that reverse engineering or independent derivation alone is not improper means. The Morlife court observed that under this statutory definition, simple disclosure or use may suffice to create liability, and that it is no longer necessary to show that the purpose to which the information was put outweighs the interests of the trade secret holder.

SOLICITATION IS "USE"; MERELY ANNOUNCING A NEW AFFILIATION IS NOT SOLICITATION
The California decisions have treated a former employee's solicitation of customers with the aid of a trade-secret customer list as a "use" of the trade secret. In Morlife, Inc. v. Perry, the Court of Appeal observed that while California courts have been reluctant to impose an unconditional prohibition on doing business with a former employer's customers, they have prohibited the use of trade secrets to solicit those customers, and that decisions both before and after the statute have equated acts of solicitation with use or misappropriation of protected information. The court drew the definition of solicitation from the California Supreme Court's decision in Aetna Building Maintenance Co. v. West -- to appeal to, apply to for obtaining something, ask earnestly, or ask for the purpose of receiving -- and repeated that court's contrasting statement that merely informing a former employer's customers of a change in employment, without more, is not solicitation. The Morlife court then described American Credit Indemnity Co. v. Seaquist, the defendants argued that the identities of the plaintiff's customers could not be a trade secret because they were readily ascertainable from trade directories, telephone books, and similar sources. The Court of Appeal rejected the argument as a matter of statutory text. The Uniform Trade Secrets Act as proposed by the National Conference of Commissioners on Uniform State Laws defines a trade secret as information deriving value from not being generally known to, "and not being readily ascertainable by proper means by," others; when the California Legislature enacted the definition as Civil Code section 3426.1, subdivision (d)(1), it deleted that phrase. The court declined to follow an earlier decision (American Paper & Packaging Products, Inc. v. Kirgan) to the extent it suggested otherwise. In a footnote, however, the court explained -- citing the Legislature's committee comment -- that the assertion that a matter is readily ascertainable by proper means remains available as a defense to a claim of misappropriation: if the defendants could show that the customers were easily identifiable and that their knowledge of the plaintiff's customers came from that identification process rather than from the plaintiff's records, the defense would rest on the absence of misappropriation rather than the absence of a trade secret.

expectedJSON.body: The second statutory requirement is that the information be the subject of efforts that are reasonable under the circumstances to maintain its secrecy. In Morlife, Inc. v. Perry, the Court of Appeal found substantial evidence of such efforts where the company's president described the customer information as its main asset, the information was stored on a computer with restricted access, the sales representative's employment contract contained a confidentiality provision expressly referring to customer names and telephone numbers, and the employee handbook stated that employees were not to use or disclose the company's confidential information after their employment, expressly including lists of present and future customers. The court cautioned that labeling information a trade secret or confidential does not conclusively establish that it is one, but treated such labeling as an important factor in showing the value the employer placed on the information and that it could not be readily derived from public sources. The court also repeated an earlier holding that, to afford protection to the employer, the information need not be in writing but may be in the employee's memory.

expectedJSON.body: Proving that a customer list is a trade secret is only the first step; the owner must also prove misappropriation. The statute defines misappropriation to include acquisition of a trade secret by a person who knows or has reason to know it was acquired by improper means, and disclosure or use of a trade secret without express or implied consent by a person who, among other alternatives, used improper means to acquire it, or who at the time of disclosure or use knew or had reason to know that his or her knowledge of it was acquired under circumstances giving rise to a duty to maintain its secrecy or limit its use. "Improper means" is defined to include theft, bribery, misrepresentation, breach or inducement of a breach of a duty to maintain secrecy, or espionage through electronic or other means -- but the statute expressly provides that reverse engineering or independent derivation alone is not improper means. The Morlife court observed that under this statutory definition, simple disclosure or use may suffice to create liability, and that it is no longer necessary to show that the purpose to which the information was put outweighs the interests of the trade secret holder.

citations.quote: Disclosure or use of a trade secret of another without express or implied consent by a person who: (A) Used improper means to acquire knowledge of the trade secret; or (B) At the time of disclosure or use, knew or had reason to know that his or her knowledge of the trade secret was: (i) Derived from or through a person who had utilized improper means to acquire it; (ii) Acquired under circumstances giving rise to a duty to maintain its secrecy or limit its use; or (iii) Derived from or through a person who owed a duty to the person seeking relief to maintain its secrecy or limit its use

expectedJSON.body: The California decisions have treated a former employee's solicitation of customers with the aid of a trade-secret customer list as a "use" of the trade secret. In Morlife, Inc. v. Perry, the Court of Appeal observed that while California courts have been reluctant to impose an unconditional prohibition on doing business with a former employer's customers, they have prohibited the use of trade secrets to solicit those customers, and that decisions both before and after the statute have equated acts of solicitation with use or misappropriation of protected information. The court drew the definition of solicitation from the California Supreme Court's decision in Aetna Building Maintenance Co. v. West -- to appeal to, apply to for obtaining something, ask earnestly, or ask for the purpose of receiving -- and repeated that court's contrasting statement that merely informing a former employer's customers of a change in employment, without more, is not solicitation. The Morlife court then described American Credit Indemnity Co. v. Sacks, in which a former sales employee's letter to about 50 policyholders announcing her new agency, inviting them to learn more about its policy, and followed by telephone calls, was held to go beyond a professional announcement and to amount to solicitation. In Morlife itself, a letter that promised to continue solving the customers' roofing problems and urged them to talk soon, followed by telephone calls and personal visits, was likewise found to be solicitation. The court noted in a footnote that, because the conduct before it was solicitation, it did not need to decide whether the professional-announcement exception has continued vitality under the statute's expansive definition of misappropriation.

expectedJSON.body: An earlier decision, Moss, Adams & Co. v. Shilling, had held that an employee largely responsible for securing a former employer's customers could solicit their continued patronage after leaving, reasoning that the employee's personal relationship with the customer negated the information's trade secret status because the employee could not be made to wipe his or her memory clean. The Morlife court rejected that reasoning on two grounds. First, on the merits, it agreed with American Credit Indemnity Co. v. Sacks that the distinction between former employees who personally dealt with customers and those who did not rests on an unsound premise: there is no legitimate reason to treat differently a former employee who uses customer information he or she personally developed for the employer and a coworker who uses the same information without ever having had customer contact, and the information developed by an employee about the employer's customers represents an investment of time and money on the part of the employer. Second, and independently, the court held that Moss, Adams was decided on events predating the Uniform Trade Secrets Act and was unencumbered by the statute's definition of misappropriation, so that its premise is inapposite to conduct occurring after the statute's effective date.

expectedJSON.body: Business and Professions Code section 16600 provides that, except as otherwise provided in its chapter, every contract by which anyone is restrained from engaging in a lawful profession, trade, or business of any kind is to that extent void, and directs that the section be read broadly to void any noncompete clause in an employment contract, no matter how narrowly tailored, that does not satisfy a statutory exception. The customer-list decisions operate on a different footing: the relief described in Morlife rested on the statutory prohibition of trade secret misappropriation, not on a contractual promise not to compete. The Morlife court described the resulting line in the injunction it affirmed: the former employees were enjoined from doing business with the 32 customers they had unlawfully solicited and from soliciting any customer of whom they acquired knowledge while employed, but the injunction did not cover potential customers with whom they had no contact and about whom they acquired no information while employed, and it left them free to solicit customers whose identities were not the former employer's trade secrets. The court also noted that under Civil Code section 3426.2, subdivision (a), an injunction's duration is not necessarily forever and that its termination could be sought under that provision.
